To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

‘Individual variation in reactions to aposematic prey exists among naive bird predators, and it can be explained by the influence of personality, a heritable complex of correlated, consistent behavioural traits’.

(a) personality affects the way in which naive individuals of a bird predator react to a novel aposematic prey; (b) fast explorers are less warily and learn to avoid aposematic prey slower than slow explorers; (c) fast explorers forget their previous experience faster than slow explorers.

(i) personality matters in reactions of naive predators to aposematism; (ii) personality types differ in their unlearned reactions to aposematists and in rate of avoidance learning; (iii) the differences in unlearned reactions may be explained by the differences in boldness, which is a component of the personality type.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel approach that links personality and predator–prey coevolution.
the question of whether personality matters when it comes to the reaction of predators to aposematically marked prey.
the role of personality in the evolution of aposematism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
individual variation in reactions to aposematic prey is a consequence of variation in personality and that personality is a heritable trait.
the variation in reactions to aposmatic prey among individuals of a bird predator is not only a result of individual experience but also an effect of personality.
personality is a significant factor that influences individual variation in reactions to aposmatic prey.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
individual personality matters in the predator–prey interactions.
individual personality traits can affect the outcome of predator–prey interactions.
personality matters: individual variation is not just a statistical artefact but may have important consequences for the dynamics of predator–prey interactions and the evolution of predator defences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
individual variation in the reactions of naive bird predator is a common phenomenon and that it may be partly explained by personality.
individual variation in reactions to aposedmatic prey exists among naive individuals.
individual variation in the reaction to novel stimuli, such as aposematism, is not only due to experience.
